meta.name: URL Shortener
meta.tagline: Turn long links into short ones and redirect millions of clicks fast. Index, Base62 codes, rate limits, caching, click analytics, sharding and edge redirects.

levels.name: First Short Link
levels.subtitle: One server shortens and redirects
levels.intro: Every link shortener starts as one machine that stores links and redirects.

feature.name: Shorten and redirect
feature.summary: Paste a long URL, get a 7-character code like sho.rt/aZ3kQ9x. Anyone who opens the short link is sent on to the long one.

realWorld: Reads (redirects) far outnumber writes (new links): about 10:1 here, 100:1 or more at bit.ly scale.
A $20/month VM (2 vCPU, 4 GB) running the app and PostgreSQL together redirects ~1,000 requests/s: a side project with ~100k clicks a day.
levels.story: Every link shortener starts as one machine. It stores each long URL with a short code and answers redirects. Build it, open it to the public and grow to 100 users.
levels.completionMessage: One server shortens and redirects for 100 users. Redirects are tiny (a 302 with a Location header), so the machine mostly needs CPU. Next: the links table keeps growing.

levels.name: Links Pile Up
levels.subtitle: Own database, an index, Base62 codes
levels.intro: Links pile up by the thousand, and every redirect searches the whole table.

feature.name: Bulk link creation
feature.summary: Marketing teams create links in bulk. Every new link is a row (code, long URL, created_at), and every redirect must find one row among thousands.

realWorld: ByteByteGo's estimate: 100M new links a day ≈ 1,160 writes/s. Over 10 years that is 365 billion rows × ~100 bytes ≈ 36.5 TB.
With short_code as the PRIMARY KEY (a B-tree index), finding one row among billions takes a few disk reads instead of a full scan.
levels.story: Marketing teams discovered you and create links by the thousand. Your one server stores every row AND answers redirects, and each redirect searches the whole table. Give the data its own machine.
levels.completionMessage: The links live in their own database, found by primary key in about a millisecond. Codes now come from unique IDs in Base62 instead of hash-and-check. Next: not everyone creating links is human.

levels.name: Spam Wave
levels.subtitle: Rate-limit link creation at an API gateway
levels.intro: Spam scripts create 30 junk links for every real one.

feature.name: Shortener under spam
feature.summary: Spammers found your free API. Scripts create thousands of links to hide phishing pages. Every spam link is a database write and a row on your disk, and it earns nothing.

realWorld: Bitly and TinyURL limit link creation per API key and IP (a token bucket, e.g. 100 links/hour on free plans) and answer "429 Too Many Requests" beyond it.
They also check new long URLs against phishing and malware lists (like Google Safe Browsing) before creating them.
levels.story: Spam scripts are hammering POST /api/shorten: about 30 spam links for every real one. Your database is busy writing junk and your disk fills with it. Put a gateway at the front door.
levels.completionMessage: Every API call now passes a gateway that counts requests per client. Scripts get "429 Too Many Requests" before they reach your app, and your disk only holds real links.

levels.name: Scale Out
levels.subtitle: Stateless app servers behind a load balancer
levels.intro: A news site sends you 1,500 users, and one crash breaks every link.
levels.story: A news site now shortens every article link with you: 1,500 users. No single app server is that big, and when your only one crashes, every link on the internet that points at you breaks.
realWorld: A redirect needs no session or user state, so app servers are stateless: any server can answer any request, and you add or remove them freely.
Behind an AWS Application Load Balancer, an Auto Scaling group adds servers when average CPU passes ~60% and replaces ones that fail health checks.
levels.completionMessage: Several stateless app servers share the work and the load balancer skips any that crash. Need more capacity? Add a server.

levels.name: Viral Links
levels.subtitle: Cache the hot links
levels.intro: A link went viral: the same few codes are clicked over and over.
levels.story: A celebrity posted one of your links. Clicks jump by half and now outnumber new links 60 to 1, and most of them ask for the same few codes. Every one still goes to your single database.
realWorld: Link popularity is very skewed: a tiny share of links gets most clicks. A Redis cache with a few GB of hot links answers 90%+ of redirects from memory (well under 1 ms).
Mappings almost never change, so cache-aside with an LRU eviction and a long TTL works with little invalidation.
levels.completionMessage: Hot links are answered from memory. The database now only sees cache misses and new links, so it stays calm even when a link goes viral.

levels.name: Click Analytics
levels.subtitle: Count every click through a message queue
levels.intro: Customers want click counts, and every click now writes to your database.

feature.name: Click analytics
feature.summary: Customers pay to see how many people clicked their links. Right now every redirect also runs UPDATE clicks = clicks + 1 on the database before answering.

realWorld: Each redirect publishes a small click event (code, time, country, referrer, device) to Kafka and returns at once. Stream processors (Flink, Spark) aggregate them into an analytics store like ClickHouse.
Bitly reports billions of clicks a month: far more click events than links. The analytics pipeline is bigger than the shortener itself.
levels.story: Analytics launched: every click must be counted. The cache answers redirects, but each one now also writes to the database, so your quiet database is suddenly drowning in writes.
levels.completionMessage: Redirects drop a click event in the queue and answer straight away. A worker folds 50 events into one database write. Clicks are counted without slowing anyone down.

levels.name: Billions of Links
levels.subtitle: Shard the database, one global ID generator
levels.intro: Links pour in by the million: one database can’t hold them, and shards clash.

feature.name: Partner API
feature.summary: Social networks and email tools now shorten every link they send. New links pour in faster than one database disk can hold.

realWorld: Hello Interview sizes 1B links at ~500 GB: one big machine could hold it, but write volume and growth push you to shard by short code (hash(code) mod N, or consistent hashing).
Unique IDs come from a central counter (Redis INCR or a ticket server, each app server taking 1,000 at a time) or from Twitter Snowflake-style IDs built from time + machine + sequence.
levels.story: Partners create links by the million. Your database disk is nearly full and no single machine is big enough. Split the links across several databases (shards), and make sure codes stay unique across all of them.
levels.completionMessage: Links are spread over several shards, each holding a slice. A single ID generator guarantees that no two links ever get the same code, and expiry keeps the tables from growing forever.

levels.name: Go Global
levels.subtitle: Redirect at the edge, 301 vs 302
levels.intro: 60% of clicks come from far away and wait 120 ms before reaching you.
levels.story: Your links are clicked worldwide: 60% of clicks come from other continents and wait ~120 ms just to reach your servers. A redirect should feel instant.
realWorld: Edge platforms (Cloudflare Workers, Lambda@Edge) answer popular redirects from 300+ cities in under 20 ms and stream each click to the analytics pipeline.
A 301 is cached by browsers, so repeat clicks never reach you: cheaper, but invisible to analytics. Most shorteners use 302 (or 301 with a short Cache-Control) to keep counting.
levels.completionMessage: Redirects are answered close to every user, clicks are still counted, and your origin only sees misses and new links. That is the architecture behind bit.ly and TinyURL.

1.hint: Users stop growing at your server's limit. Open Server and upgrade the part marked "runs out first".

1.label: Store 300 short links
1.hint: Users create links over time (about 1 per 100 user-seconds). More users = more links.
Latency climbs once any part is over ~70% busy. Upgrade so 100 users use less than 80% of every part.
About 130 people use your shortener, and a spike adds 20–40% more clicks for 20 seconds. Build room for ~180 users: in Server, "Can handle" should say 180+.
Profit = revenue − server running cost − outage penalties. Failed redirects earn nothing, so fix overloads fast. Bigger parts cost more every minute.

2.label: Move the links to their own database server
2.hint: Open Server → Database tab, buy a database server and place it next to your app server.

2.label: Make short codes from unique IDs (Base62)
2.hint: Right now each new code is a hash of the long URL, so the app must ask the database "is this code taken?" before saving. Server → Code fixes → Base62 makes the code from the row's ID: unique by design, no check needed.
Two machines now: check which one (App or DB) "runs out first" in the Server Builder.

2.label: Store 3,000 short links
2.hint: Links pile up fast now. When the disk is full every new link fails. SSDs are fast but small; NVMe holds more; HDDs are big but slow.
Without an index the database reads every row to find one code, and that gets slower with every link. Buy the Primary-key index (Server → Code fixes) and keep every part under ~75%.
Two servers means two running bills. Code fixes are a one-time cost and make every request cheaper.

3.label: Put an API gateway in front of your API
3.hint: Open Server → Gateway tab and place it. Every API call passes through it, and rate limiting rejects clients that create too many links.

3.label: Block 20,000 spam requests
3.hint: Once the gateway is in place it rejects ~95% of spam calls with "429 Too Many Requests". The counter goes up by itself.
Spam eats database writes and disk space that real users need. Block it first, then grow.

3.label: Under 1% failed requests with 600+ users
3.hint: If errors stay high, check the disk (spam fills it) and which machine runs out first.

3.label: Survive a spam attack (under 5% failed requests)
3.hint: During an attack spam traffic triples or quadruples. With a rate-limiting gateway it barely matters; without one, your database drowns in writes.
Spam never pays. Every spam link that reaches your database costs a write and disk space.

4.label: Add a load balancer
4.hint: Open Server → LB tab and place it. Then the App tab lets you add more app servers behind it.

4.label: Run 3 app servers
4.hint: Server → App tab → "Add app server". Redirects carry no session, so any server can answer any click. With 3, one can crash and two cope.
Add app servers instead of buying bigger ones. The database may need its XL parts.
When one app server dies, the load balancer sends its users to the others. They need enough spare room to take the extra load.
More servers means more running cost. Medium servers in a group are often cheaper than maxed-out ones.

5.label: Put a cache in front of the database
5.hint: Open Server → Cache tab and place it. Redirects check the cache first; only misses reach the database.

5.label: Cache hit rate 90% or more
5.hint: A few viral links get most clicks, so a cache that holds just the hot links answers almost every redirect.
App servers scale out, but there is one database. Let the cache take the clicks.

5.label: Database CPU under 50% with 2,500+ users
5.hint: With a 90%+ hit rate the database only sees 1 click in 10, plus new links.
Answers from memory are fast. Keep every machine under ~70% busy.
A cache is cheap compared to a bigger database. Spend where it helps the most.

6.label: Send click events through a message queue
6.hint: Open Server → Queue tab and place it. Redirects drop an event in the queue and answer at once; a worker counts clicks in batches.

6.label: Count 50,000 clicks
6.hint: Clicks are counted as long as redirects succeed. Failed redirects are clicks you never see.
Counting each click inline is a database write per redirect. The queue turns 50 clicks into one write.
An inline click write makes every redirect wait for the database. Through the queue, redirects return straight away.
Spikes push 1.5–2× the traffic for 20 seconds. Keep headroom on every machine.
Customers pay for analytics, but only if counting clicks doesn't cost more than it earns.

7.label: Split the links across 3 database shards
7.hint: Server → Database tab → "Add shard". Each shard holds a slice of the links (by short code), so you get 3 disks and 3 CPUs.

7.label: Add a global ID generator
7.hint: Each shard counts its own IDs, so two shards can hand out the same code. Open Server → IDs tab: one counter for everyone.

7.label: Create 10,000 links on 2+ shards with no clashing codes
7.hint: Counts new links only while you run 2+ shards and no two can get the same code: that needs the ID generator (or hashing with a check on every shard, which is slow).
New links pour in. Watch the disk: shards add space, and "Expire old links" keeps tables from growing forever.
Every shard is another running bill. Expiring old links can save you a shard.

8.label: Redirect at the edge with a CDN
8.hint: Open Server → CDN tab and place it. Popular redirects are answered in a city near each user.
With the edge answering most clicks, your origin sees far less. Check what still runs out first.
60% of clicks come from far away and pay ~120 ms. Only answering at the edge brings that down.

8.label: Click counts 95%+ accurate with 5,000+ users
8.hint: A 301 lets browsers skip you on repeat clicks: less load, but those clicks are never counted. Keep 302 (Code fixes) and keep failures low.
Spikes push 1.5–2× the traffic for 20 seconds. Keep headroom on every machine.
The edge answers most clicks, so origin servers can be smaller. Fewer, smaller machines = lower running cost.

1.text: Hi, I'm Archie! Let's build a link shortener like bit.ly. It starts as one machine that stores links and answers redirects.
Tap Server at the bottom to open the Server Builder.

A server is 4 parts: CPU does the work, RAM holds users in memory, Storage saves the links, Network sends responses. Redirects are tiny, so CPU matters most. Pick parts and press Buy. (Closed it? Tap Server again.)
Now click the glowing slot to place your server.

Your server does two things. POST /api/shorten saves a long URL and returns a short code. GET /{code} looks the code up and answers 302 Found, sending the browser on to the long URL. Clicks (reads) far outnumber new links (writes). Users also bring you coins.
To finish this level, complete every goal in Goals. Each has a hint, and any i button explains more. Your server costs coins every minute. I'll tell you when a part gets busy.
That's vertical scaling: making the one machine bigger. Each time a part fills up, upgrade the one that runs out first. Check Goals for what's left.

2.text: Level 2! Marketing teams create links in bulk: 2.5× more new links. Every redirect must find one row among thousands, on the same machine that runs your code. Give the links their own database.
Tap Server. The builder now has tabs: App server, Database and Code fixes.
On the Database tab, build a database server. Disk space matters now: every link is a row. (Closed it? Tap Server again.)
Click the glowing slot to place the database. It connects to your app server automatically.

Now watch the links table grow. Without an index, every redirect reads every row to find one code, and every new link first checks "is this code taken?". Bigger machines only buy time: look at Code fixes. I'll tell you when something gets busy.
Each time something fills up, ask: bigger machine, or better code? The index finds a code in ~1 ms; Base62 codes need no "is it taken?" check. Keep an eye on disk space. Check Goals.

3.text: Level 3! Spam scripts found your free API: about 30 spam links for every real one. Each is a database write and a row on your disk, and they never pay. Put an API gateway at the front door.
Tap Server. It opens on the new 🚦 Gateway tab.

The gateway looks at every API call (spam too), so it needs some CPU. Its rate limiting lets each client create only so many links per minute and answers the rest with "429 Too Many Requests". (Closed it? Tap Server again.)
Click the glowing slot to place the api gateway. It connects itself.
Spam now bounces off the gateway before it reaches your app or your disk. Watch the blocked counter in Goals, and get ready for a spam attack.

4.text: Level 4! A news site shortens every article with you: 1,500 users, more than any one app server can take. And when your only app server crashes, every short link breaks. Time to scale out.
Tap Server. It opens on the new ⚖️ LB tab.
The load balancer spreads requests across app servers and skips any that are down. It is light work: a small one is fine. Bigger XL parts also unlocked (dashed cards). (Closed it? Tap Server again.)
Click the glowing slot to place the load balancer. It connects itself.
Now add app servers: Server → App tab → Add app server. A redirect needs no session, so any server can answer any click (they are stateless). Aim for 3.

That's horizontal scaling with stateless servers: add one whenever you need more. Links keep piling up: Expire old links (Code fixes) keeps the table from growing forever. Check Goals, and watch for crashes.

5.text: Level 5! A link went viral: clicks are up 50%, and most of them ask for the same few codes. Every click still hits your one database. Put a cache in front of it.
Tap Server. It opens on the new ⚡ Cache tab.
A cache is mostly RAM: it keeps the hot code → URL pairs in memory. Because a few links get most clicks, even a small cache answers 90%+ of redirects. (Closed it? Tap Server again.)
Click the glowing slot to place the cache. It connects itself.
Redirects check the cache first; only misses reach the database. Check the hit rate and the database CPU in Goals.

6.text: Level 6! Customers want click analytics. Right now every redirect also writes clicks = clicks + 1 to the database before answering. That's a database write per click. Add a message queue.
Tap Server. It opens on the new 📨 Queue tab.

A queue (like Kafka) is an append-only log: redirects drop a small click event in and answer straight away. A worker reads events in batches and writes one row per 50 clicks. It needs RAM and network more than CPU. (Closed it? Tap Server again.)
Click the glowing slot to place the message queue. It connects itself.
Clicks are now counted asynchronously: the user never waits for analytics, and the database sees 50× fewer writes. Check Goals.

7.text: Level 7! Partners create links by the million. One database disk can't hold them all, and no machine is big enough. Split the links across several databases: shards.
Open Server → Database tab → Add shard. Each shard holds a slice of the links, picked by a hash of the short code, so you get more disks and more CPUs. Aim for 3.

⚠️ Problem: each shard counts its own IDs, so shard 1 and shard 2 can both make code aZ3kQ9x. That's a clash: one link breaks. (Hashing instead means checking every shard on each new link.) You need one ID generator for everyone.
Tap Server. It opens on the new 🔢 IDs tab.

The ID generator is a tiny machine (think Redis INCR): every new link asks it for the next number, so codes are unique across all shards. Later, Hand out ID ranges (Code fixes) lets each app server take 1,000 at a time. (Closed it? Tap Server again.)
Click the glowing slot to place the id generator. It connects itself.
Links are split across shards by code, and one counter keeps every code unique. Each shard adds disk space and write capacity. Check Goals.

8.text: Level 8! Your links are clicked worldwide: 60% of clicks come from other continents and wait ~120 ms before your servers even start. Answer redirects at the edge, near each user.
Tap Server. It opens on the new 🌍 CDN tab.
The CDN answers popular redirects from a nearby city and logs each click to your queue. About 80% of clicks never reach your servers. (Closed it? Tap Server again.)
Click the glowing slot to place the cdn. It connects itself.
Code fixes now has a 301 / 302 switch. A 301 lets browsers remember the redirect: less traffic, but you stop seeing those clicks. Customers pay for click counts, so choose carefully. Check Goals.

db.job: Stores every link (code → long URL) and finds one by its code.

cache.job: Keeps hot code → URL pairs in memory, so most redirects never reach the database.

cdn.job: Answers popular redirects from servers near each user, and logs the clicks.

gateway.job: Front door for every API call. Rate limiting stops scripts creating thousands of links.

storage.whatItDoes: Where the links are saved so they survive a restart. Its speed decides how many reads and writes per second it can do.

network.whatItDoes: The pipe between your server and the internet. Redirects are tiny (half a KB), so the network is rarely the problem here.

index.name: Primary-key index
index.short: Make short_code the table's primary key (a B-tree), so the database jumps straight to one code instead of reading every row.
index.effect: Database CPU, disk reads and latency stop growing with the number of links. Each new link costs a little more (the index is updated too).

storage.title: 💾 Storage
storage.body:
Where data is saved so it survives a restart. Here: every short link (code, long URL, created time), roughly 100–500 bytes a row.

Disk speed (operations per second) decides how fast rows are found and written. Disk space decides how many links fit.

Real world: 1 billion links ≈ 100–500 GB, which fits on one SSD. 365 billion (ByteByteGo's 10-year estimate) ≈ 36.5 TB does not.

feature.title: How the shortener uses your server
feature.body:
• POST /api/shorten: save a long URL, return a 7-character code. A write: CPU and a disk write.
  • GET /{code}: find the code, answer 302 Found with Location: https://the-long-url. A read: CPU and a lookup. The response is tiny.

Reads (clicks) outnumber writes (new links) 10:1 here, and 100:1 or more in real shorteners. So the read path is what you optimise: index, cache, edge.

database.title: 🗄️ Database server
database.body:
A machine whose only job is the links: storing them, finding one by its code.

Table: urls(short_code PRIMARY KEY, long_url, created_at, expires_at). A relational database (PostgreSQL, MySQL) is a fine choice: writes are few, lookups are by key.

Splitting it off means the app server stops spending CPU, RAM and disk on data, and each machine can be sized for its own job.

diskSpace.title: 💽 Disk space
diskSpace.body:
Every link is a row on the database disk. Links are usually kept for years, so the table only grows.

When the disk is full, every new link fails. Fixes: a bigger disk, more shards (Level 7), or expiring old links.

Sizes are game-scaled (shown as how many links fit) so disks fill in minutes instead of years.

index.title: 🔎 Primary-key index
index.body:
Like the index at the back of a book. Without it, to find code aZ3kQ9x the database reads every row (a full table scan), and that gets slower with every link.

With short_code as the primary key (a B-tree), a lookup takes a few steps even among billions of rows: about a millisecond.

Cost: each new link also updates the index, so writes get a little slower. For a read-heavy shortener that's a great trade.

base62.title: 🔤 Base62 short codes
base62.body:
Two common ways to make a short code:

  • Hash the long URL (MD5, CRC32) and keep 7 characters. Codes can clash, so you must check "is this code taken?" before saving, and retry on a clash.
  • Encode a unique ID in Base62 (0-9, a-z, A-Z): ID 11157 → 2TX. Unique by design, so no check is needed.

7 Base62 characters = 62⁷ ≈ 3.5 trillion codes. The catch: the IDs must be unique across every machine that makes them (see Level 7).

cache.title: ⚡ Cache
cache.body:
Memory in front of the database (Redis, Memcached) holding hot code → long URL pairs. Redirects check it first; only misses go to the database (cache-aside).

Link popularity is very skewed: a few links get most of the clicks. So a cache holding a small share of links can answer 90%+ of redirects.

A link almost never changes once created, so there is little to invalidate. Use LRU eviction and a TTL no longer than the link's expiry.

cdn.title: 🌍 CDN / edge redirects
cdn.body:
Servers in hundreds of cities. With edge code (Cloudflare Workers, Lambda@Edge) they can answer a popular redirect right next to the user, without crossing an ocean.

Each edge logs the click to your analytics queue, so counts stay right. New links and unpopular codes still go to your servers.

redirect301.title: ↪️ 301 vs 302
redirect301.body:
301 Moved Permanently: the browser remembers it and goes straight to the long URL next time. Less load, but you never see repeat clicks.

302 Found (temporary): every click comes back to you. More load, but every click is counted, and you can change or expire the link later.

Shorteners that sell analytics (like bit.ly) use 302, or 301 with a short Cache-Control.

expiry.title: ⏳ Link expiry
expiry.body:
Store an expires_at on each link. Expired codes answer 410 Gone, and a nightly job deletes them (or a lazy check on read).

The tables stop growing forever, so you need fewer shards and disks.

clickAnalytics.title: 📊 Click analytics
clickAnalytics.body:
For every click: which code, when, from which country, referrer and device. Customers pay to see these counts.

Writing a counter inline makes each redirect wait for a database write. Instead, send an event to a queue and let a worker count in batches.

Real world: Kafka → Flink/Spark → ClickHouse or Druid. The analytics pipeline often ends up bigger than the shortener itself.

spike.name: Shared on a forum
spike.story: One of your links is on the front page of a forum.

spike.name: Influencer post
spike.story: An influencer put your short link in their bio.

spike.name: Breaking news
spike.story: A news alert with your short link went out to millions of phones.

bots.name: Spam attack
bots.story: A spam network is creating phishing links through POST /api/shorten.

bots.name: Botnet
bots.story: Thousands of hijacked machines are calling POST /api/shorten in a loop.

crash.name: App server crashed
crash.story: One of your app servers ran out of memory and crashed. It is restarting.

crash.name: Hardware failure
crash.story: A disk died in one of your app servers. It is being replaced.
